strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Running a family office with more than USD 1 billion under management now costs USD 6.6 million a year, J.P. Morgan's newest survey finds, and only 14 per cent have a written plan for replacing the people who run it
lead.standfirst: J.P. Morgan's 2026 Global Family Office Report puts a price, for the first time at this scale, on what it costs simply to keep a family office running, and finds succession planning for the office itself lagging far behind its own governance.
lead.body:
J.P. Morgan Private Bank's 2026 Global Family Office Report surveyed 333 single family offices, 197 based in the United States and 136 elsewhere, across 30 countries, together representing more than USD 500 billion in wealth. The average office in the sample runs USD 1.1 billion in assets under management for a family with an average net worth of USD 1.6 billion, and for the first time at this scale, J.P. Morgan has put a price on what it costs simply to keep that infrastructure running.

The costs rise sharply with size. An office overseeing USD 250 million or less spends around USD 875,000 a year to operate, rising to USD 1.7 million between USD 250 million and USD 500 million, USD 3.2 million between USD 501 million and USD 999 million, and USD 6.6 million once assets under management pass USD 1 billion. A family office, in other words, now has a cost curve as legible as a household's own payroll, and one that grows in the same direction.

Staffing that cost is where the report finds its widest gap. A chief executive or president sits atop 36 to 42 per cent of the offices surveyed, a chief financial officer in 20 to 32 per cent and a chief investment officer in 24 to 31 per cent, yet only 14 per cent of offices have a defined succession planning process for those roles, meaning 86 per cent would be improvising the day a senior executive left. Eighty two per cent maintain a formal investment committee and 80 per cent outsource at least part of investment management, evidence of real institutional structure sitting above a leadership bench nobody has actually planned to replace.

The family office has, in the space of a few reports like this one, become a staffed institution in its own right rather than a back office attached to the family, complete with a payroll, an org chart and now a documented cost of running it. For household staff and estate managers who sit alongside that office rather than inside it, the report is a reminder that the professional standard being set at the top of a family's operation, in governance, in succession, in cost discipline, is the same standard increasingly expected of the house itself.
lead.why: The family office is now costed and governed like any institution, and the succession gap showing up in its own leadership bench is the same gap recruiters have long described in the household, a reminder that professionalisation is arriving from both directions at once.

articles.title: More than a third of family offices report recruiting difficulty this year, a new compensation survey finds, and the chief financial officer has become the hardest role of all to fill
articles.body:
Botoff Consulting's 2026 Compensation and Talent Planning Survey, described by the law firm Katten as the most expansive proprietary dataset focused on family offices, finds recruiting has become the year's central operating problem rather than a peripheral one. More than a third of participating offices reported difficulty filling roles over the past year, a challenge that grows more acute, not less, at the largest and most complex offices.

The single hardest role to fill is the chief financial officer, particularly one who combines strategic planning with tax and estate planning expertise, and the survey finds a broader accounting talent shortage running across the sector. The underlying cause is less a shrinking pool of candidates than a widening one of employers: a surge in new family office formation, layered on top of the generational succession already reshaping who runs existing ones, has pushed demand for experienced talent well ahead of the supply able to meet it.

Compensation structure is moving to compete for that talent. Discretionary, one off bonuses are giving way to structured annual incentive plans built around individual performance, organisational results and investment performance metrics, and long term incentive plans, deferred compensation, co-investment and carried interest among them, are extending down into family office pay for the first time, a structure historically reserved for hedge funds and private equity firms.

For household staff and estate managers who often report through, or alongside, the family office, this is the vocabulary they are increasingly expected to share. Performance metrics, deferred compensation and carried interest used to belong only to the investment side of a family's operation, and are now part of how the whole household is being asked to think about pay.
articles.why: As family offices adopt structured, performance linked pay to compete for scarce financial talent, the household staffing market that estate managers and butlers enter is being pulled toward the same vocabulary and the same discipline.

articles.title: The global superyacht order book has fallen 4 per cent to 1,093 vessels, new industry data show, even as Italian yards tighten their grip on more than half of everything on order
articles.body:
Boat International's Superyacht Global Order Book 2026, presented locally by the Italian boating association Confindustria Nautica, counts 1,093 yachts on order worldwide, down 4 per cent from 1,138 a year earlier. Italy's own share of that order book rose two percentage points to 52 per cent, meaning 568 of the yachts currently under construction anywhere in the world are being built on an Italian slipway.

The decline in raw numbers sits alongside continued financial health among the yards themselves. Half of the shipyards surveyed reported turnover increases over the past year and a quarter reported stability, while roughly half kept their own order books at prior year levels and a quarter grew them, a pattern that reads less like a market in retreat than one consolidating around fewer, larger and more complex builds.

The scale behind those figures is considerable. Italy's wider nautical sector generated EUR 13 billion in added value in 2024 and employed 168,000 people, with headcount growing 5.6 per cent even as the number of yachts on order declined, a sign that much of the industry's value now sits in outfitting, systems and refit work rather than in hull count alone.

For the crew and shoreside teams a concierge eventually coordinates around a family's yacht, a smaller but more concentrated order book means a longer wait for a new build slot but a deeper, more specialised Italian supply chain, from carpentry to systems integration, to draw crew and after sales service from once she is delivered.
articles.why: A smaller but more concentrated order book, deepening in Italy specifically, is the same supply chain a concierge draws on for crew placement, refit scheduling and after sales service long after a yacht is delivered.
articles.src: SuperYacht24, citing Boat International and Confindustria Nautica

articles.title: Online interest in residency and citizenship by investment has risen more than eightfold in a decade, new research finds, as Malta's programme closes and Argentina prepares to open one
articles.body:
Analysis published in September by CEOWORLD magazine finds search interest in residency by investment and citizenship by investment programmes has risen more than eightfold over the past ten years, with more than 100 countries now operating some form of investment migration scheme.

Portugal remains the preferred destination for American and British applicants through its EUR 500,000 investment visa route, with Malta and Italy named as established alternatives. Malta's own decade old scheme, which generated EUR 1.4 billion over its lifetime, closed in 2025 following a European Union court ruling against it, removing one of Europe's longest running routes at the same moment that Greece and Panama are gaining attention, the latter through a USD 300,000 real estate route.

The market's next entrant may be its largest single economy yet. Commentary accompanying the research points to an expected citizenship by investment programme from Argentina before the end of the year, which would mark a materially larger economy entering a field so far dominated by small states and city economies.

Each of these programmes converts, on the ground, into a household opened or a household relocated, the estate manager's own paperwork mirroring the investor's, and Malta's closure is a reminder that the mobility a family buys can be legislated away almost as quickly as it was created.
articles.why: Every residency route opened or closed here is, in practice, a household being built or wound down elsewhere, work that lands on estate managers and staffing agencies long after the investment decision itself is made.

articles.title: A single 1980 Diego Giacometti console fetched close to USD 4.6 million in Paris last month, leading a run of autumn sales in which documented history, not rarity alone, decided the result
articles.body:
At Sotheby's Paris, a 1980 bronze console table by Diego Giacometti, titled Homage to Boecklin and sold as part of the Rochas Collection, achieved roughly USD 4.56 million, reinforcing how strongly the decorative arts market continues to reward single owner, well documented design furniture over comparable pieces without a clear history.

In New York, Christie's dispersed the complete 181 print Alan Medaugh collection of Hiroshige woodblocks for a combined USD 6.99 million. A single sheet, Plum Estate, Kameido, took USD 358,400 against an estimate of USD 60,000 to USD 100,000, a result the house's specialists attributed to the rarity of finding the set intact rather than to any single image.

Both results extend a pattern running through the month's design and Asian art sales more broadly, in which an unbroken, well kept chain of ownership is doing more to move a price than the object's rarity on its own.

For whoever manages a family's collection, the lesson across an entire season's results is consistent. A console or a print set with clean, complete paperwork is outperforming rarer or equally fine objects without it, which makes the private collection manager's own records as much a driver of value as the object in the vitrine.
articles.why: Across an entire season's results, documented provenance is doing more to move a price than rarity alone, which makes the private collection manager's own records part of what a family's holdings are actually worth.

briefs.b: Business jet flights rose 4 per cent worldwide in the first half of 2026 to 1.95 million departures, led by North America's 5 per cent growth and 72 per cent share of all flights. Fractional ownership was the most dynamic segment, up 11.5 per cent, with NetJets alone accounting for 13.6 per cent of global departures, while flying in the Middle East fell 17.8 per cent amid geopolitical tension.

Liv-ex's midyear data show the broad fine wine market barely moving, its flagship Liv-ex 100 index up just 0.4 per cent so far in 2026, while Italy's own index rose 1.5 per cent on the strength of Tuscan names such as Soldera Case Basse and Masseto, some vintages of which gained more than 20 per cent over the year. Bordeaux, by contrast, slipped 0.3 per cent over the same period.

New research from AlTi Tiedemann Global and Campden Wealth, surveying 126 family offices between February and May 2026, finds 48 per cent have now formally defined their wealth's purpose, up from 33 per cent a year earlier, most often to guide the next generation. Yet 71 per cent admit they have not yet fully engaged that next generation in the conversation.

A 1982 Rickenbacker 330 guitar played by Johnny Marr on Oasis's Definitely Maybe sold at Christie's London for roughly USD 474,500 against an estimate of USD 79,000 to USD 105,900, another instance this season of a well documented history moving a price several times past its estimate.
